misconceptions.say: On $[0,1] \cup (2,3]$: it is not an interval, and the two open sets $(-1, 1.5)$ and $(1.5, 4)$ intersected with the space split it into two non-empty open pieces.

On $\Q$: take any irrational $\alpha$ and split at it. $\{q \in \Q : q < \alpha\}$ and $\{q \in \Q : q > \alpha\}$ are open in $\Q$, disjoint, non-empty, and together they are all of $\Q$ — because no rational equals $\alpha$. $\Q$ is in fact **totally** disconnected.
On the discrete metric: every subset is open, so pick any non-empty proper subset and its complement. A discrete space with more than one point is as disconnected as a space can be.

feedback.nudge: Three of the five come apart, and in each case you can write down the two open sets that do it. The two that do not are a continuous image of an interval and the standard example of a space held together by a limit point.

distractors.0: No. Take $U = (-1, \tfrac32) \cap E$ and $V = (\tfrac32, 4) \cap E$: both are open in $E$, disjoint, non-empty, and their union is $E$. It is not an interval, which already settles it.
distractors.1: No. For any irrational $\alpha$, the sets $\Q \cap (-\infty, \alpha)$ and $\Q \cap (\alpha, \infty)$ are open in $\Q$, disjoint, non-empty and cover it. $\Q$ is totally disconnected: its only connected subsets are the single points.
distractors.2: Yes. The circle is $g\bigl([0,2\pi]\bigr)$ for the continuous $g(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$. $[0,2\pi]$ is an interval, hence connected, and a continuous image of a connected space is connected. It is also path connected, which gives the same conclusion.
distractors.3: No. In a discrete space every subset is open, so any non-empty proper subset and its complement disconnect it. A discrete space is connected only when it has at most one point.
distractors.4: Yes — and this is the point of the example. It is connected: the graph part is a continuous image of $(0,1]$, hence connected, and the whole space is contained in its closure, which keeps it connected. It is **not** path connected: no continuous path can get from the segment to the graph, because approaching $x=0$ the second coordinate oscillates between $-1$ and $1$ for ever.

explanation:
## The line, settled completely

A non-empty subset of $\R$ is connected **exactly when it is an interval** — where "interval" includes single points, rays and all of $\R$. One classification, and both of the subsets of $\R$ here fall out of it: $[0,1]\cup(2,3]$ has a gap and $\Q$ has a great many.

The proof of the hard direction is the one worth remembering. If $E$ is not an interval there are $a < c < b$ with $a, b \in E$ and $c \notin E$; then $E \cap (-\infty, c)$ and $E \cap (c, \infty)$ disconnect it. Finding a missing point in the middle is all that disconnecting a subset of the line ever requires.

## Continuous images

$f$ continuous and $X$ connected implies $f(X)$ connected. The proof is two lines through preimages: a disconnection of $f(X)$ pulls back to a disconnection of $X$.

That single fact does a great deal of work:

- the circle is connected, being the image of $[0, 2\pi]$;
- the intermediate value theorem is the special case $Y = \R$: a connected subset of $\R$ is an interval, so a continuous function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$;
- anything path connected is connected, since a path is a continuous map from an interval.

## Connected without being path connected

The topologist's sine curve is the standard example, and it is standard because it is the *simplest* one.

It is connected: the graph $G = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \le 1\}$ is a continuous image of $(0,1]$ and so is connected, and the whole space $S$ satisfies $G \subseteq S \subseteq \overline{G}$ — every point of the segment is a limit of points of the graph, because $\sin(1/x)$ takes every value in $[-1,1]$ on every interval $(0,\eps)$. A set squeezed between a connected set and its closure is connected.

It is not path connected. A path from a point of the segment into the graph would have to be continuous at the moment it leaves $x = 0$, and in any neighbourhood of that moment the second coordinate must swing from $-1$ to $1$ infinitely often. No continuous function does that.

So connectedness is strictly weaker than path connectedness. They coincide for **open** subsets of a normed space (Theorem 5.3.7 in the notes, which is marked non-examinable) — and the sine curve is not open, which is why it is allowed to exist.
